title: Patrick N Ward and Andy Day

sentences.text: Yeah, I'm good, thank you.
Yeah, it is.
Afternoon.
Where are you?
I'm based in.
Just outside of London.
There's a place called Somerset.
Don't know if you've.
This meeting is being recorded.
You've heard of it at all?
I have not.
What's your side?
That's the only thing that matters in these conversations.
What's your football side?
I'm not much of a soccer fan, unfortunately.
So which is yours?
Cottenham Hotspur?
Spurs fan?
Fair enough.
Yeah.
My dad was fan, so fair enough.
This year.
This year it's bad news.
It's been awful, awful, awful.
We'll see what happens in the Euros.
Otherwise it's been awful.
Yeah.
That's a shame.
But it's good to meet an American that's a soccer fan as well.
So, yeah, it's.
I'm kind of a die Hard.
I like play fantasy with a bunch of guys in England and I'm a big fan of England.
I love it very much.
Love it very much.
As much as I care.
As I would like.
Where's your.
Where's your place in the uk?
Is there somewhere that you visit or.
London.
Mostly London, Devon, but mostly London.
Mostly London.
I don't get back as much as I would.
I have four very, very good friends who are English.
One's from Devon, one's from Wales, ones from the Midlands.
And I don't know where Tony's from.
I can't remember where Tony's from, but they are.
Three of them live here.
One of them still lives in London.
He lives in Islington.
So, yeah, we're quite close to Devon, actually.
So Devon's there.
Oh, are you the next county along?
Yeah.
Oh, right.
I may be there this summer.
I don't.
My wife doesn't want to let me go, but I want to go because my one.
My dear friend who grew up in Devon, his eldest daughter, is getting married and she's.
She's having, you know, the modern way that kids get married now.
She's having a.
She's having a party in Chicago, where her fiance is from, and then a party at her home in New York in suburban New York, and then a party in Devon.
I honestly don't know, Andy, where she's getting married.
Probably Devon.
You would hope.
You should hope.
Yeah.
But I don't think so because I think, you know, she's.
She's definitely American.
Grew up in California.
And then her parents.
And then she moved to New York to be a filmmaker, and then she.
And then her parents moved to New York because her sister is also.
Who's my goddaughter actually her sister's a, a theater performer and so they're both in New York.
They don't have any.
Palo Alto is not a place for them to be.
Right.
To pursue those careers.
So.
And so she's got.
Think she's got a lot of friends in New York and I think it's.
I don't know if this is the same.
I doubt it is in England as it is here.
But here the, the, the trend has decidedly moved towards the wedding being the kids, the actual bride.
Like when I was a kid and when I got married the wedding was really your parents event.
You know.
And so all their friends came and, and your parents basically said okay, you can invite 10 people or you can invite.
And then I'm going to invite 50.
Right.
And that's flip flopped and now it's the kids invite everybody and then the parents get to maybe invite a few people.
So I think that she's gonna, I think that's what's happening.
Anyway, enough about my friends and weddings in England.
So, so tell me about your.
You and your service and I'll.
And I'll give you a bit of background on why I'm curious about it.
Yeah, sure.
So.
So we are capital A and we're an M and A advisory for marketing services businesses.
So all of our clients are buying or selling marketing agencies and we work on the buying the sell side.
So the sell side we have agencies co which is the mailing list I think you responded to and that that's a platform for a marketplace for buyers and sellers and marketing agencies.
We work on the buy side as well with clients usually sort of high growth agencies or investors or private equity.
And we're also doing our own roll ups as well.
So we kind of get to see all of all areas of the industry deals from every angle.

And my, my thing really is working with founders and helping them get the best value out of the deals that we do because it's, it's a place where a lot of bankers or private equity investors make a hell of a lot of money off people without having to do very much.
So I'm here to inform and help and leverage and make sure that my clients get the best deals if they're selling or if they're investing etc.
So yeah, very much that I'd love to Hear more about 104West what it is that you're thinking about and be happy to help you as well.
Definitely.
Sure.
So, so let Me give you a little bit of background and I'm going to, because I have this, for some reason this insane soft spot for English people.
I'm going to trust you on some, I'm going to trust you and bringing into my confidence on some things just to so.
And all of this is probably easy enough to, to glean with a modicum of research, but I'll do it anyway.
So.
So we're 20 years old.
We basically function almost exclusively in the tech business.
And when I say almost exclusively that the outliers are always tech adjacent in some way, shape or form.
But we do have an outlier every once in a while.
So a toy company, for instance.
Right now we're dealing with a, a company that is actually making game spaces or is developing, you know, amusement park sorts of things, but they're all based on technology, so that kind of thing.
But the bread and butter is core enterprise technology, you know, really deep like quantum computing and you know, obviously AI today and augmented reality, virtual reality, that sort of thing.
And then you know, we'll do things as esoteric as like AI driven point of sale systems.
Right?
We are, we're, we've been as big as 18 or 20 people.
I'd say the smallest are probably pretty small right now.
We're probably about 12 right now.
1099s and W2s.
Does that distinction mean something to you?
Okay, good.
And you know, the last couple of years have been, last couple years have been rough.
We did about 2 million in 23, in 24.
We dropped significantly 25, 30% in 25.
Right now we're on, we're on the road.
If I look at Q1 as the Q1 is the first sort of indicate, leading indicator, we're on the road back to where we were two years ago.
So.
And we've got some really, there's a couple of really good things in the offing and you know, knock wood that they come through.
I am relatively convinced that the era of boutique generalist agencies in the tech world is closing, if not closed already.
I just don't think that given any number of factors, I just don't think that, you know, doing sort of legacy conventional communications tactics is worthwhile.

It just, it just, it doesn't, I mean, I think it works for some people who are very unsophisticated about what they're trying to get and have and don't understand what their outcomes are and don't really look at, they look at the function of communications as a necessity rather than as Something that they actually, they actually should be doing.
And why I think that those people are willing to put out meaningless news releases and harass the press ad nauseam for meaningless stories.
I think they'll do that till the cows come home.
Fine, go do it.

But the more sophisticated people that I talk to are much more concerned with how do I integrate what I'm doing in communications with the rest of my go to market efforts and how do I try and create more opportunities using communications and more measurable opportunities using communications than simply just use it as a kind of reflex mechanism.
Right.
We talk a lot about reactive versus proactive communications.
Right.
Is your communications tied to what happened in the business or is your communications tied to what you want to happen in the business?
In other words, are you trying to do something.
I've often used that use the analogy or the metaphor of are you using a sword or a shield?
Right.
If you're using a shield to just sort of protect yourself in the marketplace, you probably don't want to talk to us.
If you're using a sword and you're trying to cut through the marketplace, that's where we're going.
And you know, we truly believe that.
To use another metaphor, to mix them up as many, as much as I can.
This is a gardening metaphor.
It sort of appeals to the English.
Not like the sword fighting one didn't.
But, you know, we're not really interested in somebody who wants us to come and tend their garden.
Right.
If you, if you're, if you're like, if you're happy with your, with what you're doing, then why are you looking for a new agency?
Right.
I always say to my, my team that when we're going into new business, I always say, listen, I've never met a future client, a potential client who was happy with what was going on.
They're not happy with their agency.
If they're, if they're, if they're leaving their agency and trying to do something new, clearly they're unhappy.
But many of them will feign discomfort or dis, dis discontent and, and then actually just go right back to where they were.
We just did a pitch with, with, with DoorDash.
They were, they were asking, they were looking for an agency for all of their enterprise stuff.
In other words, their conversations with their, with their restaurants, the B2B part of what Door Dash does, not the beat at the consumer side.
And they were like, yeah, we really want to do some interesting stuff.
We really want to do.
And we came to them with really interesting and smart.
It was too smart.
Plan built around the data that comes off the platform.
Right.
I mean, when you think about it, doing Doordash knows more about what people eat than anybody on the planet.
Like Kroger's or San Sainsbury could tell you what people buy, but Jordache tells you what they eat because nobody orders from Doordash and then doesn't eat it.
Right.
Lots of stuff happens with Sainsbury where you buy stuff and you don't use it.
Right.

So we tried to use that and we went through this whole thing about how you can tell what's happening in a marketplace, how you can tell what's happening in trends and how you can tell what's happening, and then feeding all that back to the, to the restaurant and using that as a way to really cement your relationship with the restaurant, really accelerating and helping their business, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera.
And they came back to us and they said, well, but how are you going to get publicity for our restaurant owners?
And we just went, wow.
Really?
Really?
That's what you're interested in?
So, so that, that's a bit of our color, a bit of our culture.
I don't know if that's helpful, but.
Where, where you guys are coming from, for sure.
So, so what are you looking to do?
So you've been around for a while.
Are you looking to sell or.
Or do you have something else in.
In mind?
So I, I need to give you one more piece of information which I think is going to be helpful and, and probably elucidating.
So we joined a.
A holding group called Next Practice Group two years ago, almost two years ago, and it was a catastrophe, Just an absolute catastrophe.
It was catastrophic.
From like, the whole thing's blown up.
This is not public, but if you basically snooped around, you'd figure it out.
The whole thing just went, as you English like to say, tits up.
Excuse me, if that's a little bit.
If that's a little bit offensive.
And, and so I have a very bad taste in my mouth for acquisitions right now.
We're not in a place.
Our books look like crap.

After the last two years, our books look like crap, principally because we were led to believe by a person who put our deal together was, you know, a peer of yours, if you will, maybe not a peer, but does the same thing you do.
And they assured us that, you know, getting into this deal would accelerate our abilities to attract a certain kind of, you know, go upstream a little bit.
We do a lot of Work in early stage.
Right.

And we're trying to do so startups and things like that and we're trying to do a little bit more work in sort of either higher price tag programs with larger companies or a little bit more steady and you know, easy.
What's the word I'm looking for?
Steady or more predictable work from a mid tier company.
Right.
And we were assured by these guys that they were going to help us do that and they did absolutely nothing.
And so I took my eye off the ball for 14 months, 16 months and hurt us bad.
And so, and so we're rebuilding.
So we're not in a, we're not in a place to do anything soon.

But the reason I'm curious or the thing that I'm interested in thinking about is a roll up because I, you know, we've done a lot of work in data driven communications and I'm personally convinced that one of the great holes in most communications programs is audience insight and research, understanding who you're talking to and why.
I think a lot of communications is essentially throwing darts at a board and seeing where it hits and hoping that, that and then measuring it on the back end.

I think mostly especially from a content point of view, I think we, we as an industry do a reasonably good job of understanding who consumed a piece of content and who consumed, who participated in a program in the past tense.
But we don't do a very good job of targeting and understanding who are the people we're trying to go after.
And this may not be as true in consumer or it may not be as true in some other practices, but in tech it's pretty true.
Specifically in enterprise.

The enterprise, from a sales and from a marketing point of view, the world is so finite and so well known that they do a really good job there with things like ABM and whatever of targeting who that is.
But they don't bring any of that into communications for some reason.

So they don't really understand, you know, they'll, they develop programs and they don't use any of the, any of the Personas or any of the characteristics or any of the market behaviors that they so absolutely feast on in the sales and the marketing side.
They don't bring any of it into communications.
And so I think that there's an opportunity to, to, to sort of produce a little bit more of that.
I also think there's an opportunity for greater sophistication in the communications effort.
You know, and this is, I'm not talking about sort of the, the larger enterprises or The Salesforces and the Adobes and the saps and the Ciscos, those guys are, that's a different world.
But the mid tier, the mid tier sort of, they fly blind in communications.
They just, they don't know what they're, who they're talking to or what they're saying.
And it's all, we make this distinction between storytelling and story making.
Right.
And the concept of storytelling is like this reactive thing, like oh well, we opened a new office, we find hi to hired a new cfo, we have this new product.
And what we advocate is that's fine, you can do that, you need to do that.

But you probably need to think also and maybe even more about how are you creating narrative, how are you story making that is well informed, knows who the audience is, is reiterating the issues and, and, and problems and challenges are happening in a marketplace through the prism of the company that you're talking to and sort and creating the kind of, the kind of engagement that attracts the audience as opposed to just is throwing stuff at them.
And so, so I've got a, I've got a few targets that I'm thinking about.
But my conversation, what I was hoping to kind of have conversation with you about was to really understand at a more a macro level sort of where you think the communications agency marketplace is.
You said about private equity.
I mean, I get five calls a week from private equity.
The only thing that outpaces the private equity calls is the people who claim that they can get me 15 new sales calls a week.
Right.
And I'm suspicious, I'm wildly suspicious of the latter and fairly suspicious of the former.
Okay, so where is the market?
I would say the market is pretty good.
You know, it's at the bottom end of the market is always a fast moving place.
It doesn't really matter what's going on in economics or the world at large, because it is fairly private.
The buyers and sellers, they're not private equity businesses.
They usually people who are entrepreneurial and they're growing the business.
So a buyer of 104 west in particular, while you were, you know, doing a couple of million in revenue would most likely be another agency that's looking to grow in a certain area.
Private equity, they do do bolt ons with businesses that are doing less than 5 million.
But, but it's, it's less of that.

So really the, the end goal would probably be to build something that private equity would be more interested in because what happens is the private equity buyers push up the market values, the Valuation businesses.
So for instance, if, if you went to market, you probably be able to command a 4-6x multiple on the business somewhere in that range on top or bottom line on bottom on ebitda.
So you not give me your margins, but assuming it's around 20, 30%, so you would get a multiple of that usually low single digits.

And the strategy that I'm helping a lot of, you know, founders in your own position is, is to see if there is a roll up opportunity where you can exit with, with sort of low double digits rather than single digits.

So you know, if you can build a business that's somewhere in the region of sort of 10 to 20 million in revenue with the 20, 30% margin, you're more likely to be somewhere in the range of 8 to 12, let's say.
So the opportunity is there for smaller agencies to join together and create something that is more sellable with a bigger pool.
And basically the private equity buyers, they will push up the price from that 4 to 6 range to much higher.
So that's, that's the, you're saying that.
You use the, you use the private equity as kind of a pawn a beard in the, in the process to essentially just raise the price from acquiring agency?
Well, not really.
I mean they do raise the prices.
It's not, it's not sort of a bait and switch to try and push the price up artificially, but it just is because they're in the market.
The big, the bigger buyers push the price of the market up so the multiples are stronger the, the larger the EBITDAR is.

So if you can pull that together with five or six agencies and get somewhere towards, you know, sort of 5 to 8 million EBITDA for instance, that then once you get there, the economics really change and you are able to command those double digit valuations, you know, in the, the 10 to 12 range for sure.
So, so our strategy has been to help 1 million EBITDA businesses to get to that stage and to group them together.

But certainly if you were looking to do a more strategic roll up, the economics aren't as greatly sort of magnified but certainly you would have a much better exit multiple if you could find some other agencies to roll up with it.
And from what you're saying, I'm, I can see you're passionate about the, you know, you have a strategy about how you can amplify each other's work by working together.
And also there would be some, some economic uplift as well by just being part of a bigger business.
So.
Right.
Patrick, so are you thinking that you would like to sort of head up a roll up and do something along the lines of what you were involved in with, with next practices, obviously?
No, not with it.
Because that was, that was strategically from a, from an operating point of view that was just a, that was just a show.
So.
No, nothing like that.
Thank you.
I mean from the, from there.
Yeah, yeah, I know.
I kind of achieved.
I had to get that.
Yeah, that was like.
I'm sorry, that was sort of just.
A problem with bankers is they.
They do.

And it's particularly bad in, in marketing more than anything else because they don't understand the nuances between marketing businesses that they could be hugely different businesses but, but look very similar from the outside.
And so the financial investors unfortunately have come into the industry and it up a load of times.

It's not, it's not the first time and certainly they are still at it, rolling up 10 businesses that are nothing like each other, that anybody that works in marketing could identify that, but they're just unable.

Well, I mean the current vision that I'm kind of playing with is that, you know, I have two, I, you know, I have two partners and there's a third that I'm, that I'm meeting with and I have a couple of other people in this, in that world.
As I say, I'm very cynical about the traditional communications function inside of a regulatory, relatively successful technology community, technology enterprise.
I don't think what we want to do is really a communications thing.
I think it's, I think it's.
For me, I.
This is how I was explaining it to someone recently.
If I describe something to you, that said, we have deep insights about the market, deep insights about the audience.
We develop, we develop ammunition.
We develop assets that are akin, that are, that are derived from that intelligence.

We then deploy those assets through every channel we can get to and then we measure the daylights out of it on the back end to understand efficacy and success and then basically turn that around and do it again.
Does that sound like communications to you?
Doesn't sounds like marketing to you.
But the assets we're talking about are not ads, they're not direct mail.
They're different kinds of narrative assets of story making.
And so we're just toying with the idea and I'm curious what your thoughts would be.
We're trying to understand how to shape this in a way that says what we're doing is much more.
It's closer to business, it's closer to marketing, it's closer to sales enablement.
It's closer to sales support than it is classic communications, which I find a reactive process and, and essentially not something anybody's that interested in.
I, I worry that that concept is so unorthodox that a kind of normal buyer looks at and goes, I don't know what the hell that is.
So sorry to stop you, but I've got another call.
No worries.
Which I'll have to hop onto.
But I want to finish your point before I do.
So the thing is, I think, Patrick, if you are interested in exiting your business, I think there's a strong market for PR companies.
We've listed a few and we've got one now which is just a tiny little regional business, and there's interest in that.
We've actually got somebody that's looking to buy it and bring it in house and, and do something with it with some military businesses that, that they're working on.
It's completely different from what the, the agency is doing at the moment, but there is a, a buyer for it is my point.
I think where you are at the moment and the fact that you're working with these tech companies probably leaves you open to a lot of interest.
There would be a lot of potential buyers, but it's all about what you feel happy about exiting the business at.
And so it's more about, you know, what do you want from it?
If you feel that you're.
I mean, because it sounds like you're extremely passionate about what it is that you're talking.
No, I really don't care.
It's really okay.
You're a good actor.
I'm very passionate about it.
The Hollywood vibes.
But.
But yes, certainly if you are passionate, you can.
You have a vision of why these companies do fit together and maybe somebody else can't see it.
I think there's also a market for that.
Like I said, if you can get to a bigger scale, then the companies become more valuable anyway.
But certainly private equity are probably, you know, they're going to be blind to the differences between what PR and marketing.
Yeah, they just care about money.
They just care about.
Also from the outside, it is all marketing.
It's just different channels.
So.
So from their point of view, they're not going to be that bothered about the differences that you're talking about and whether those pieces fit together.
So there would be certainly a buyer at the end of it that would be happy to invest more money and time into helping to grow that business.
Once you've got it to a certain point.
And then within the industry, perhaps it would muddy the waters because a lot of people do buy in the way that you're already thinking about.
You know, people will come to us and say we need a PR company.
People will come to us and say we need a performance marketing or we need ad network tech, you know, or whatever.
It's always a very specific buyer.
They're looking for creative shops or, or a social media arm.
So from that point of view, it does become more difficult to sell a business that seems difficult to understand from within the industry.
But I think, I think it's becoming less of that.

There is a convergence of sorts and certainly AI is accelerating that and everybody is looking at all marketing, including pr, because we're seeing a convergence of PR and social media companies, for instance, which seemed very disparate types of companies five or ten years ago, certainly.
But now we see a lot of PR companies and social media companies either merging or growing out of the same.
So I think things change over time.
I think if you are interested, I'll be happy to have another call because obviously we've run out of time.

But if you're interested in talking about how we can help you make those acquisitions or, or help you with that merger, then certainly there are things that we can help you with and I'll be happy to talk in more detail about them if that's the, the route that you want to go down.

So probably best if I follow up with an email explaining what we do a little bit more clear, clearly, maybe, and then we can set up another time if that's something that you're, you're definitely looking to pursue.
I think that my intention from this was to meet each other, see if there was, for lack of a better word, chemistry.
See if there was, you know, if we, you know, if I.
There was something that we could potentially, like we wanted to do something together, potentially.
I mean, obviously we're not committing to anything, but whatever.
And so.
So that's what I would like to think about you about that too, and let me know and I'll let you know.
I'm.
This is a long game.
This is not something that's going to happen in six months.
So.
So this is the beginning and if, you know, we.
I need to hone this and I need to figure out what the offering really looks like.
And then I need to work with my partners and see if they're interested in putting it together.
I know that the two main ones are not.
They're under 2 million, so they've got nowhere to go.
They need to do something.
Yeah.
So that's the opportunity.
I mean, obviously I'm seeing it from slightly more from the financial side, because that's a big part of what we do, is making sure things line up like that.
But I think that's the big opportunity for you and your partners is like you said, I mean, there are buyers for smaller agencies, for sure.
Absolutely.
We've sold a tiny one in Los Angeles last year that it looked like a complete basket case from the outside, but we had like 45 signed NDAs in 24 hours.
So there is a buyer for every business.
So it's not just they're small and nobody's going to buy them.
That's not the case at all.
But the economics change for everybody and if you want a bigger exit, then certainly engineering something like this with a group of people is the.
The way forward.
So why not put something in the email?
Because I've got a hug, so I'm six minutes late for my.
Sorry.
No worries, mate.
Listen, but could you also let me know about a few structures, please?
Yeah, sure.
I can.
I can put something in there.
We've got a couple of different ways to get started on some different things, so.
Yeah, I'm sure you do.
Let's put.
Just to let us understand it, so.
Yeah, great.
It was wonderful meeting you.
Yeah, good to meet you too, Patrick.
Enjoy the rest of your day.
Thanks, Sandy.

summary.overview: In the Business Development Consultation meeting between Patrick N Ward and Andy Day, key insights were exchanged regarding the M&A landscape for marketing services businesses. Andy Day introduced Capital A's role in connecting buyers and sellers, emphasizing their commitment to securing the best value for agency founders. Patrick shared an overview of his agency, 104West, a tech PR firm recovering from a recent downturn, and discussed its unique focus on proactive communication strategies. Both parties identified strategic challenges facing boutique agencies, including market shifts favoring targeted audience insights. They explored the potential for a roll-up strategy involving complementary agencies and assessed the strong M&A market for PR firms, noting the advantages of larger combined entities. Action items included Andy providing more detailed information about Capital A's services and deal structures, while Patrick would consider future collaboration and refine his business approach.
summary.short_summary: In a recent consultation, Patrick N Ward and Andy Day discussed the M&A landscape for marketing services, with Andy outlining Capital A's role in facilitating connections between agency buyers and sellers. They emphasized the importance of securing optimal value for agency founders. Patrick provided insights into 104West, his tech PR firm that is recovering from a downturn, and detailed its focus on proactive communication strategies. The conversation also pinpointed strategic challenges faced by boutique agencies, particularly in adapting to market shifts that favor targeted audience insights. They explored the feasibility of a roll-up strategy involving complementary agencies and noted the robust M&A market for PR firms, highlighting the benefits that larger, combined entities can offer. Action items included Andy's commitment to deliver more information on Capital A's services and deal structures, while Patrick would contemplate future collaboration and refine his business strategy.
